read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "Hebrew WordNet exact Princeton WordNet 3.0 synset alignment and English gloss" (M43): 4,174 routes (axis: routes), 3,194 letters keys (axis: keys). The source audit (builder/02-audit.mjs, evidence about the source and no part of any test): the source is the Hebrew WordNet of the Open Multilingual Wordnet joined to the data files of Princeton WordNet 3.0, in ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/omw-hebrew-pwn30-2026-07-14/. Through the dictionary store's records every one of the 4,174 routes is tied to one synset, and the record's gloss equals the text after the bar on its line of the source's data file on 4,199 of 4,199 records. The route equals the source's whole gloss on 2,283 routes and is the gloss less its example sentences on 1,891; no route is anything else. So a route comes from one field and no test here stands on a guess about a field. The source's own key is on file in the same folder, in WordNet-3.0.tar.gz: the manual pages doc/man/wndb.5, doc/man/wngloss.7 and doc/man/wninput.5. They say that each synset has one gloss, a text string that provides a definition of what the synset represents, example sentences, or both. They name no sign inside a gloss; a search of what they say on a gloss (builder/02-audit.mjs, source-audit/key-search.json) finds no line that names a comma, semicolon, colon, hyphen, slash or quotation mark, and the round brackets they name are the ones the lexicographer's file puts round the whole gloss, which reach no route. So every shape's meaning here begins "unverified:".

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one index of the JavaScript string: every route holds only characters of 16 bits. A letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}), of any script and either case. A digit is one of the ten characters 0 to 9. Whitespace is what JavaScript's String.prototype.trim removes, and trimmed means with that removed from both ends. The text is the whole route text as it stands, the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def. The text before and the text after the mark are the template's c.before and c.after, never trimmed unless the test says so. What a bracket holds is the template's c.group, the same for an opener and for its closer, and it is not trimmed. Empty means no character at all. Directly before and directly after name the one character next to the mark; at an end of the text no character stands there, so a test that asks for a character there fails. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it, and a full stop after » belongs to the sentence. Every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character, and no test matches part of a string in a list. The apostrophe in every string is the straight one, U+0027, the backtick is U+0060, and the double quote is U+0022. No test uses a class of case. Two tests that compute a string: THE PIECE AFTER THE MARK: take the text after the mark; if it holds a comma or a semicolon, of any container, keep only what stands before the first of them; trim that; keep its first 40 characters, or all of it if it is shorter; do not trim again, so the result may end in a space. THE FIRST WORD: of a named text, the run of letters and digits that starts at its first character, empty if that character is neither a letter nor a digit or the text is empty; the first word after the mark is the first word of the trimmed text after the mark. THE WORD ROUND THE MARK: three runs put together with nothing between them, the run of letters that ends directly before the mark, the mark itself, and the run of letters that starts directly after the mark; either run may be empty.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. A shape's container field is not part of its test unless the test says so. An occurrence that no shape of its mark takes makes the classifier throw. Not caught above means the shapes listed above it for the same mark.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source tells two meanings under one Hebrew word apart by the synset's number, and the route store does not carry it; the dictionary store's record keeps it (its loc). The source's own files carry that id and the store dropped it. By the audit each text under a key comes from one synset, and on all 644 of the 644 keys with more than one text each text is a synset of its own (axis: keys; example key אישית). WordNet does not separate homonyms from senses: a synset is one meaning, however its words are related, so this count holds both.

branches.question: Some rows give two wordings of one meaning, with a semicolon, a comma or a colon between them: make free from confusion or ambiguity; make clear. In this dictionary a row is one meaning of the word, so by the source's own account the second wording offers no different meaning. No sign in the row can tell a second wording from a note, so these rows were picked by hand. Today the page never cuts at a semicolon or a colon, and it cuts at a comma where a piece is short. Should these marks cut the row? From the day this is wired, each of these rows prints whole. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other question, and each answer cuts only at its own marks.

options.means: The page prints each wording as a reading of its own: make free from confusion or ambiguity and make clear. It cuts only at these marks. A word like or that opens a wording stays in it, and a label or a note stays with the wording it stands beside, even where it speaks of both.
The page prints each row as one reading, as written: make free from confusion or ambiguity; make clear. For a row with a comma that the page cuts today, this is a change from today.
